Buckle up for the week of the year.

9 days ago, President Trump threatened to "stop trading" with all countries that the US has a trade deficit with if the Fed does not CUT rates.

On Wednesday, the Fed will release their September interest rate decision.

Currently, markets believe the Fed will HIKE rates on Wednesday.

In other words, the market now expects Fed Chair Warsh to make the exact opposite policy decision that President Trump wants, just 3 months after he was appointed.

If the market is correct and President Trump follows through on his threat, global trade is about to take a major turn.

This move would effectively cut off trade with ~50% of all US trading partners, including Mexico, China, Taiwan, Germany, Japan, South Korea, Canada, and India.

Turn on our post notifications at @KobeissiLetter to receive real time analysis as the week progresses.

tweets.text:
It seems most people don't understand how severe the energy situation is right now in the Middle East.

As of Friday, Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline has officially been shut down after recent attacks, putting -4 million barrels of daily oil exports at risk.

Meanwhile, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait is now at risk of being shut down, threatening up to -9 million barrels of daily oil supply.

All while the Strait of Hormuz is operating at ~20% of its pre-Iran War capacity, removing -15 million barrels of daily oil flows.

Combined, this represents nearly ~30 MILLION barrels per day of oil flows that are either offline or at risk.

Even after accounting for some overlap between these routes, the scale of the potential disruption is enormous relative to the ~100 million barrel per day global oil market.

This is one of the most severe energy supply situations in modern history.

tweets.text:
Silver miners are sitting on a record cash pile:

Net cash balance across the top 10 silver mining companies surged to a record ~$4.2 billion in Q2 2026.

This figure has more than doubled since Q3 2025.

This marks a sharp reversal from the 2014-2024 period, when debt exceeded cash levels for most quarters.

To put this into perspective, during the 2010-2011 rally, combined net cash balance among these companies never exceeded $2.0 billion.

Cash accumulation has accelerated sharply alongside the silver rally, as higher silver prices have boosted margins and free cash flow across the group.

Silver miners have never been this liquid.

One of the more interesting things happening in the economy right now is the tug-of-war between housing and AI-related business investment.

Housing has been weak for years, and normally that kind of weakness would be a major recession warning.

But housing is only one part of the economy’s cyclical engine.

Durable goods consumption has been improving, while business equipment investment has accelerated sharply, led by computer equipment tied to the AI capital spending boom.

So while housing is moving in one direction, AI-related investment is moving strongly in the other.

Residential investment, durable goods consumption, and business equipment investment together make up what I call Cyclical GDP. These areas are only about 20% of the economy, but they drive most of the booms and busts.

So far, strength in durable goods and business equipment has been enough to more than offset the weakness in housing.

Housing weakness still matters. But housing by itself has not been enough to push the broader economy into a downturn.

If the Fed starts raising rates again, that will put further pressure on the housing sector. The key issue is not whether housing keeps contracting, but whether housing weakness eventually becomes strong enough to pull down the economy’s cyclical engine.

That would turn today’s tug-of-war into a much broader cyclical problem.

For now, the cyclical economy as a whole is turning higher after a multi-year soft patch.
